claim: Binge alcohol consumption represents a large proportion of the deaths associated with problematic alcohol use.
source: Binge alcohol consumption, defined as consuming 4–5 or more drinks in about 2 hr for females and males, respectively, represents a large proportion of the deaths associated with problematic alcohol use and is one of the strongest risk factors for developing alcohol use disorder (AUD) (Mokdad et al., 2004; Addolorato et al., 2018; Kanny et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mokdad et al., 2004; Addolorato et al., 2018; Kanny et al., 2018).

claim: Binge drinking is one of the strongest risk factors for developing alcohol use disorder (AUD).
source: Binge alcohol consumption, defined as consuming 4–5 or more drinks in about 2 hr for females and males, respectively, represents a large proportion of the deaths associated with problematic alcohol use and is one of the strongest risk factors for developing alcohol use disorder (AUD) (Mokdad et al., 2004; Addolorato et al., 2018; Kanny et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mokdad et al., 2004; Addolorato et al., 2018; Kanny et al., 2018).

claim: Binge drinking is particularly prevalent among young adults.
source: Binge drinking is particularly prevalent among young adults, especially among females who have been increasing their alcohol use rates year after year for the past half-decade that now are similar to or outpacing male use rates (Keyes et al., 2019; White, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Keyes et al., 2019; White, 2020).

claim: Females have been increasing their alcohol use rates year after year for the past half-decade that now are similar to or outpacing male use rates.
source: Binge drinking is particularly prevalent among young adults, especially among females who have been increasing their alcohol use rates year after year for the past half-decade that now are similar to or outpacing male use rates (Keyes et al., 2019; White, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Keyes et al., 2019; White, 2020).

claim: Modeling binge drinking in rodent animal models is largely accomplished through the behavioral paradigm, Drinking in the Dark (DID).
source: Modeling binge drinking in rodent animal models is largely accomplished through the behavioral paradigm, Drinking in the Dark (DID), in which mice have ad libitum access to alcohol (20% v/v) in their home cage for 2 hr sessions, 3 hr into their dark-light cycle for 3–4 days a week, and for one 4 hr 'binge' session for a single day, followed by 2 or 3 days of abstinence from alcohol (Rhodes et al., 2005; Thiele and Navarro, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Rhodes et al., 2005; Thiele and Navarro, 2014).

claim: The DID procedure has great construct and predictive validity for human binge drinking.
source: This procedure has great construct and predictive validity for human binge drinking.
evidence: The claim is stated as an assertion based on established knowledge about the DID paradigm.

claim: Mice display similar drinking patterns to humans like front-loading behavior wherein they consume larger amounts of alcohol early in the task compared to later in the task.
source: Mice display similar drinking patterns to humans like front-loading behavior wherein they consume larger amounts of alcohol early in the task compared to later in the task (Ardinger et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Ardinger et al., 2022).

claim: DID successfully induces pharmacologically relevant levels of blood alcohol content (BAC) in mice that is equivalent to the legal intoxication limit in humans.
source: DID also successfully induces pharmacologically relevant levels of blood alcohol content (BAC) in mice that is equivalent to the legal intoxication limit in humans (Barkley-Levenson and Crabbe, 2014; Huynh et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Barkley-Levenson and Crabbe, 2014; Huynh et al., 2019).

claim: Female mice tend to drink more than males across a wide range of alcohol consumption models, including DID.
source: It is also commonly observed that female mice tend to drink more than males across a wide range of alcohol consumption models, including DID (Blednov et al., 2005; Hwa et al., 2011; Satta et al., 2018; Sneddon et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Blednov et al., 2005; Hwa et al., 2011; Satta et al., 2018; Sneddon et al., 2019).

claim: Females tend to drink more than males due to an increased sensitivity to the rewarding and decreased sensitivity to the aversive properties of alcohol.
source: Possible reasons are that females tend to drink more than males is due to an increased sensitivity to the rewarding and decreased sensitivity to the aversive properties of alcohol, different pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of alcohol, and differences in sex hormone expression levels, such as estrogen which fluctuates across the menstrual cycle (Czerniak, 2001; Overstreet et al., 2004; Schramm-Sapyta et al., 2009; Finn et al., 2018; Sneddon et al., 2019; Vandegrift et al., 2020; Elvig et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Czerniak, 2001; Overstreet et al., 2004; Schramm-Sapyta et al., 2009; Finn et al., 2018; Sneddon et al., 2019; Vandegrift et al., 2020; Elvig et al., 2021).

claim: There are reported instances in which male and female mice consume identical amounts of alcohol in drinking models, such as for mice genetically selected to consume high binge levels of alcohol.
source: Yet, there are also reported instances in which male and female mice consume identical amounts of alcohol in these drinking models, such as for mice genetically selected to consume high binge levels of alcohol (Savarese et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Savarese et al., 2021).

claim: There is evidence to suggest there is no effect of the estrous cycle on alcohol intake specifically during DID.
source: And, while it is known that estrogen plays a role in increasing alcohol intake in some models, there is evidence to suggest there is no effect of the estrous cycle on alcohol intake specifically during DID (Satta et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Satta et al., 2018).

claim: The neural circuitry that underlies binge drinking remains poorly understood.
source: Additionally, the neural circuitry that underlies binge drinking remains poorly understood, and descriptions of sex differences for neural circuits currently implicated in binge alcohol consumption remain even more elusive.
evidence: The claim is stated as an assertion about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Only a few studies to date have included sex as a factor in their analyses of neural circuits implicated in binge drinking.
source: Of the neural circuits implicated in binge drinking, only a few of these studies to date have included sex as a factor in their analyses (Rinker et al., 2017; Ferguson et al., 2019; Siciliano et al., 2019; Burnham et al., 2021; Dornellas et al., 2021; Levine et al., 2021; Haggerty et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Rinker et al., 2017; Ferguson et al., 2019; Siciliano et al., 2019; Burnham et al., 2021; Dornellas et al., 2021; Levine et al., 2021; Haggerty et al., 2022).

claim: Alcohol uniquely alters AIC inputs into the DLS via synaptic alterations in mu opioid and ionotropic glutamate receptors in male mice.
source: Previous work from our laboratory that investigates such circuitry shows that alcohol uniquely alters AIC inputs into the DLS via synaptic alterations in mu opioid and ionotropic glutamate receptors in male mice (Muñoz et al., 2018; Haggerty et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work from the authors' laboratory (Muñoz et al., 2018; Haggerty et al., 2022).

claim: Female mice displayed no alcohol-induced changes in ionotropic glutamate receptor function.
source: Female mice displayed no alcohol-induced changes in ionotropic glutamate receptor function.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding from previous work, implicitly referencing the authors' prior research.

evidence: The claim is stated as a finding from previous work, implicitly referencing the authors' prior research.

claim: Animals achieved stable levels of water intake across 15 water DID sessions.
source: For DID sessions in the first 3 weeks, animals achieved stable levels of water intake across 15 water DID sessions, and there were no sex differences between male and female water drinking (Figure 1c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1c-d.

claim: There were no sex differences between male and female water drinking.

evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1c-d showing mixed ANOVA results with Sex F(1,12) = 0.1032, p=0.7535.

claim: Mice reliably consumed binge-like levels of alcohol during the 4 hr sessions.

claim: There were no differences in alcohol intake between males and females across all DID sessions.

claim: There was a greater amount of alcohol drank during week 4 in comparison to week 5 for both sexes.

evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1i showing rmANOVA results with Week F(2,26) = 7.8861, p=0.002, and post-hoc comparison Week 4 to Week 5, p=0.0012.

claim: Females consumed more water between both water and alcohol DID sessions across all 6 weeks compared to males.

evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1k showing mixed ANOVA results with Sex x Drinking Week F(5,60) = 2.411, p=0.0466.

claim: Previous inter-session DID water intakes were negatively correlated to the next DID session water intake.
source: Previous inter-session DID water intakes were also correlated to the next DID session intake to see if the amount of water consumed before any water DID session had any influence on the amount of water consumed during the upcoming DID session. We found a modest, yet statistically significant negative correlation (Figure 1l).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1l showing Shepherd's pi correlation, r=–0.2383, p=0.0002.

claim: Increasing female intersession water intake is negatively and significantly correlated with lower alcohol DID intakes.
source: Yet, the patterning between males and females for thirst states looks strikingly different. While we did not find a statistically significant difference using sex as a covariate in a co-variate analysis of variance (ANCOVA) to determine if the slopes of the regression fit were statistically different, if one a priori separates sex and then runs a regression, the correlation for male intersession water intakes predicting alcohol DID intakes is not significant (p=0.0916), whereas increasing female intersession water intake is negatively and significantly correlated (p=0.0007, r=–0.4133) with lower alcohol DID intakes (Figure 1o).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1o showing correlation analysis for females only: r=–0.4133, p=0.0007.

claim: For water intake, water events, event duration, and number of drinks were all significantly correlated with intake and there were no differences in how male and female mice consumed water out of the lickometers across all DID water sessions.
source: For water events, event duration, and number of drinks, were all significantly correlated with intake and there were no differences in how male and female mice consumed water out of the lickometers across all DID water sessions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–c).

claim: For alcohol event duration and number of alcohol drinks, female mice showed an increased correlation with alcohol intake at lower event numbers and drinks compared to males, suggesting they might be more efficient drinkers.

For drinking events, there were no sex differences, yet for the alcohol event duration and number of alcohol drinks, female mice showed an increased correlation with alcohol intake at lower event numbers and drinks compared to males, suggesting they might be more efficient drinkers, such that efficiency measures the ability to consume more alcohol in a single drinking interaction compared to males (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e-f showing ANCOVA results with significant sex effects.

claim: For water intake, across DID weeks 1–3, there were no sex differences in the number of events, event durations, water events, the latency to drink water, the mean inter-drink interval between water events, nor differences in front loading behavior for water intake.

evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2a–f showing mixed ANOVA results with no significant sex effects.

claim: Both males and females displayed similar levels of front-loading behavior for alcohol.

claim: Drinking behaviors are largely encoded by male AIC inputs into the left DLS, with alcohol displaying the largest change in magnitude for ΔF/F both across time.
source: First, to summarize the differences between calcium activity at left and right inputs to the DLS, we averaged all z-scored water and alcohol drinking sessions' calcium activity and compared them for sex, fluid, lateralization, and time differences. Altogether, it showed that drinking behaviors are largely encoded by male AIC inputs into the left DLS, with alcohol displaying the largest change in magnitude for ΔF/F both across time (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3a showing ANOVA results with significant interactions.

claim: Alcohol-left male AIC inputs show the largest magnitude peak amplitude, and water-left AIC inputs the second largest when time locked to drinking events.
source: When analyzing the peak amplitude of the calcium signals, we also find that alcohol-left male AIC inputs show the largest magnitude, and water-left AIC inputs the second largest when time locked to drinking events (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3b showing ANOVA results with significant interactions.

claim: For left AIC inputs, calcium activity is increased for alcohol compared to water across time for both sexes, but especially in males.
source: By looking at all AIC inputs into the left DLS by sex and fluid, calcium activity is increased for alcohol compared to water across time for both sexes, but especially in males (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3c showing ANOVA results with significant Sex × Fluid × Time interaction.

claim: For left AIC inputs during water drinking, males show increased peak amplitudes for both water and alcohol compared to females.
source: More detailed analyses of the dynamics of the calcium signals also displayed both sex and fluid differences for the peak amplitude of the calcium signal where males show increased peak amplitudes for both water and alcohol compared to females (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3d showing ANOVA results with significant sex effect.

claim: For males, binge alcohol consumption, compared to water, increases the amount of time that it takes for the peak calcium signal to occur.
source: Interestingly, a sex-by-fluid interaction shows that for males, binge alcohol consumption, compared to water, increases the amount of time that it takes for the peak calcium signal to occur (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3e showing ANOVA results with significant Sex × Fluid interaction and post-hoc test for males.

claim: In females, binge alcohol consumption, compared to water, decreases the time to peak.
source: Whereas in females, binge alcohol consumption, compared to water, decreases the time to peak (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3e showing ANOVA results with significant Sex × Fluid interaction and post-hoc test for females.

claim: For left AIC inputs, the AUC for both water and alcohol measures were increased compared to females, suggesting that the calcium signals were larger and remained elevated for longer after the peak occurred.
source: Finally, we measured the area under the curve using ΔF/F values from the time when the peak ΔF/F value occurred to the time when the end of the drink occurred to assess the decay kinetics of the calcium signal. For left AIC inputs, the AUC measurements also showed both sex and fluid differences, such that the AUC for both water and alcohol measures were increased compared to females, suggesting that the calcium signals were larger and remained elevated for longer after the peak occurred (Figure 3f).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3f showing ANOVA results with significant sex and fluid effects.

claim: For right AIC inputs, a decrease in calcium for alcohol compared to water is present, especially in males.
source: For AIC inputs into the right DLS by sex and fluid across time, compared to the left AIC inputs, these findings are reversed, such that a decrease in calcium for alcohol compared to water is present, especially in males, and that the sex differences, regardless of the fluid consumed, are mainly driven by differences in the off-kinetics of the calcium dynamics. (Figure 3g).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3g showing ANOVA results with significant interactions.

claim: Males decrease their peak amplitude calcium signals as they transition to binge alcohol consumption at right AIC inputs.
source: In more detail, an interaction between sex and fluid for peak amplitude shows that males decrease their peak amplitude calcium signals as they transition to binge alcohol consumption (Figure 3h).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3h showing ANOVA results with significant Sex × Fluid interaction and post-hoc test for males.

claim: For right AIC inputs, females see a decrease in time to peak as they switch from water to binge alcohol drinking, yet there is no change in males.
source: For time to peak, like left AIC inputs, females see a decrease in time to peak as they switch from water to binge alcohol drinking, yet there is no change in males (Figure 3i).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3i showing ANOVA results with significant Sex × Fluid interaction and post-hoc tests.

claim: There was only a sex-dependent decrease in males compared to females for AUC at right AIC inputs, regardless of fluid.
source: Finally, there was only a sex-dependent decrease in males compared to females for AUC, regardless of fluid (Figure 3j).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3j showing ANOVA results with significant sex effect.

claim: For left AIC inputs, regardless of sex, alcohol increases calcium activity compared to water during drinking events and for right AIC inputs, alcohol decreases calcium activity compared to water drinking events.
source: In summary, two main findings are apparent, such that (1) for left AIC inputs, regardless of sex, alcohol increases calcium activity compared to water during drinking events and for right AIC inputs, alcohol decreases calcium activity compared to water drinking events, and (2) that male calcium dynamics at both left and right AIC inputs are more strongly altered by alcohol exposure than female calcium dynamics.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3 showing various ANOVA results.

claim: Male calcium dynamics at both left and right AIC inputs are more strongly altered by alcohol exposure than female calcium dynamics.
source: In summary, two main findings are apparent, such that (1) for left AIC inputs, regardless of sex, alcohol increases calcium activity compared to water during drinking events and for right AIC inputs, alcohol decreases calcium activity compared to water drinking events, and (2) that male calcium dynamics at both left and right AIC inputs are more strongly altered by alcohol exposure than female calcium dynamics.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3 showing various ANOVA results.

claim: A net shift towards increased engagement of AIC inputs into the left DLS during the transition from water to binge alcohol drinking in males, but not females, is achieved via both increasing AIC engagement to the left DLS and decreasing AIC engagement to the right DLS during drinking events.
source: Together, we also observed a net shift towards increased engagement of AIC inputs into the left DLS during the transition from water to binge alcohol drinking in males, but not females, which is achieved via both increasing AIC engagement to the left DLS and decreasing AIC engagement to the right DLS during drinking events.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3 showing various ANOVA results and comparisons.

claim: For left AIC inputs during water drinking, males show an increase in peak amplitude in week 3 compared to weeks 1 and 2.

evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4b showing ANOVA results with significant week effect and post-hoc comparisons.

claim: For the right inputs in water-drinking males, there was a decrease in peak amplitude in week 3 compared to week 1.
source: For the right inputs in water-drinking males, we saw the opposite for peak amplitudes, a decrease in week 3 compared to week 1, no change in time to peak, and a decrease in the AUC in week 3 compared to week 1 (Figure 4f–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4f showing ANOVA results with significant week effect and post-hoc comparison.

claim: Left AIC inputs for water-drinking females also increase peak amplitude, with no change in time to peak by week, like left AIC inputs in water-drinking males.
source: We see similar changes, such that left AIC inputs for water-drinking females also increase peak amplitude, with no change in time to peak by week, like left AIC inputs in water-drinking males (Figure 4j–k).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4j showing ANOVA results with significant week effect.

claim: For left AIC inputs in males during binge alcohol drinking, there was a decrease in the off-kinetics in week 6 compared to week 5 and week 4.

evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5d showing ANOVA results with significant week effect and post-hoc comparisons.

claim: While alcohol strongly encodes drinking activity during binge alcohol consumption, the calcium signal begins to decay quicker as the drinking history increases.
source: This suggests that while alcohol strongly encodes drinking activity during binge alcohol consumption, that the calcium signal begins to decay quicker as the drinking history increases.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data presented in Figure 5d showing decreased AUC in week 6.

claim: For females, across the board, a lack of alcohol-induced changes over time is observed, which can be interpreted as a resistance or insensitivity to binge alcohol consumption across time.

claim: Lateralization of insular activity is well documented in human and rat studies.

claim: This is the first demonstration, in a water or alcohol-drinking paradigm, to show lateralized effects of AIC inputs in the mouse.

claim: In previous work, lateralization effects were not seen when stimulating AIC inputs into the left DLS compared to the right DLS.
source: Also, in our previous work, we did not see lateralization effects when stimulating AIC inputs into the left DLS compared to the right DLS, but it is important to note that the time-resolution in which we were photo activating AIC inputs in the DLS was around 10 orders of magnitudes longer than the time-resolution of the measured calcium activity, suggesting we could have been occluding lateralization effects by stimulating for too long, at a non-biologically relevant frequency, and/or with too much light power (Haggerty et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Haggerty et al., 2022) and includes speculation about why lateralization was not observed.

source: Furthermore, the findings presented here help contextualize our previous work on AIC input control over binge alcohol drinking behaviors such that alcohol exposure in males decreases robust calcium activity from AIC inputs that when restored with photoactivation of AIC inputs into the DLS leads to decreases in binge alcohol consumption (Figure 5d).
